transcript:
Meeting header: 
Date: 2026-09-25 15:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Samira Ng (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (Product), Maya R. (HelixEdge ML), Derek S. (HelixEdge Infra), Priya K. (HelixEdge PM)

Summary:
Quick walkthrough of Redwood failure/fallback playbook when facing exponential session tailbacks: long conversational histories, very high TPS bursts, streaming backpressure on client connections, and timeouts. Show Console traces, Optimize recommendations, and a proposed canary rollback policy.

Topics covered:
- Long-context preservation and KV/prefix caching strategies
- Continuous batching and adaptive windowing under high TPS
- Streaming backpressure behavior and client-side retry semantics
- Timeout cascades and graceful fallbacks (smaller model, cached response, partial output)
- Operational observability: traces, token-level cost, per-route SLOs

Short action items (recorded in notes above).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Patel: All right, hi everyone, thanks for joining. We're going to do a focused run through of a few edge scenarios you mentioned in the form submission — long histories combined with bursty TPS and then what happens when streaming gets backpressured or hits client timeouts. Samira's going to drive the demo.

[00:18] Samira Ng: Hey Maya, Derek, hi Priya — quick context, we've seen HelixEdge uses cases with multi-turn agent threads that sometimes reach 120k token context sizes before you compress; is that still accurate?

[00:28] Maya R.: Yeah it's, uh, ballpark. Some of our long-running sessions for simulation logs can approach the 100k token ballpark, but we do some pruning. The problem is spikes — you can get 4–6k TPS when a user group runs batch inference.

[00:42] Derek S.: Right and our infra has a default HTTP client timeout of 60s, but a lot of the agent flows are streaming and we have intermittent mobile clients which drop mid-stream.

[01:00] Samira Ng: Cool thanks. So demo plan: 1) reproduce a long-history request and show how prefix/KV cache hits reduce compute; 2) push a high-TPS burst and show continuous batching adaptations; 3) introduce client-side backpressure and show the graceful shedding and fallback playbook.

[01:22] Jordan Patel: And as a reminder we'll highlight Console traces and Optimize suggestions — those are the main artifacts we'll share after the call.

[01:30] Samira Ng: kicking off screen — here's the Console (minor UI lag). On the left is the route config, you can see we have a model-family pinned to 'rw-large-v1' with a fallback chain to 'rw-medium-q4' and then a text-only cached store. Notice the prefix cache is enabled with a 48-hour TTL.

[01:55] Derek S.: Quick question — prefix cache, so that's per-client session or global?

[02:02] Samira Ng: It's global per-route but keyed by session namespace plus prefix hash. So multiple clients can hit the same cached prefix if they're in the same session group. That matters for your simulation jobs where identical prompts are spun up.

[02:18] Maya R.: hmm okay that could help a lot.

[02:22] Samira Ng: All right real traffic replay: I'm replaying a recorded session with a 110k token history. First request is a continue-conversation call with streaming enabled.

[02:35] [STREAM] Speaker 1: um the transcript is a bit rough but we can see token emission starting...

[02:44] Samira Ng: Console trace shows an early cache hit on the first 30k tokens due to prefix reuse — backend compute dropped from estimated 600ms per chunk to 90ms; that's the KV/prefix win.

[03:02] Priya K.: wait 90ms per chunk is realistic? are those numbers synthetic?

[03:07] Samira Ng: they're from the replay on a dedicated node we prepared — it's representative but we'll share the raw benchmark CSV. Note: when prefix hits are full, latency is dominated by the final generation window; otherwise you pay full sequence compute.

[03:25] Jordan Patel: important callout — if your KV cache keys are too granular you lose hit-rate; if they're too broad you might leak context across tenants. We recommend namespace-level separation per simulation project.

[03:40] Samira Ng: now I'm going to fire a sudden TPS spike — synthetic clients ramp from 200 TPS to 4.2k TPS over 12 seconds. This stresses the batching layer.

[03:52] [15s later sample log omitted] Speaker 2: (inaudible) um server reports queue depth rising, batching window auto-increased.

[04:10] Samira Ng: Console alert pops up: queuing latency breached soft SLO. The runtime adapts by widening the batching window to 60ms to maintain throughput; that reduces per-token cost but adds latency for some requests.

[04:28] Derek S.: If we widen batching window won't mobile clients time out?

[04:33] Samira Ng: Exactly the trade-off. We have routing policies: for premium routes you can pin to a low-latency pool (reserved capacity) which keeps batching windows narrow; for best-effort routes we widen batches. Also you can set per-route client-timeout padding — Redwood can inject keepalive frames into streams to keep TCP alive while we're batching.

[04:55] Maya R.: Those keepalive frames, are they standard SSE or chunked transfer?

[05:00] Samira Ng: chunked transfer with light ping tokens (null bytes + meta). Clients should tolerate small inter-token gaps; but as you mentioned mobile clients sometimes close due to app-level timeouts, which is where the fallback playbook comes in.

[05:16] Samira Ng: I'm going to introduce artificial backpressure: slow client that reads at 1 token/sec and then drops connection at T+18s.

[05:28] [00:05 clip of simulated stream playback] Speaker 1: okay, stream backpressure evident.

[05:35] Samira Ng: The runtime marks that session as slow reader; by default we continue to buffer up to a configurable buffer limit (we default to 8MB per session). Once the buffer threshold is crossed the runtime marks the stream as 'saturated' and starts shedding: it first trims KV history to reduce active memory, then falls back according to the route policy — first to a cached response if available, otherwise to a smaller quantized model, and finally to truncated/partial output (we send first N tokens then follow-up: see partial output option).

[06:05] Derek S.: Trimming history sounds risky for correctness. Do we get visibility into what was trimmed?

[06:10] Samira Ng: Yes, every trimming event is logged to the trace with the pre/post token ranges and reason code; Console highlights it as a yellow event and Optimize will suggest prefix sizing changes if it sees frequent trims.

[06:22] Maya R.: And when it falls back to the smaller quantized model, do we get a similarity/regression metric?

[06:28] Samira Ng: We do. Optimize runs a quick BLEU/ROUGE-ish similarity check for short form and a pretrained eval suite for longer outputs; it's logged and you can set a regression threshold to trigger an alert.

[06:40] Samira Ng: Okay continuing — in this scenario the client dropped after 18s, runtime recorded a partial output served from cache for similar earlier session — hit. The call ended; Console shows 'fallback: cache' and an SLO impact of +12ms token-latency but a 98% success rate overall.

[06:58] Priya K.: How would you recommend we configure our mobile clients? Shorter timeouts? longer?

[07:06] Jordan Patel: Best practice: set HTTP read timeout to something slightly larger than your expected batching window plus max per-token emission time. If you expect bursts that widen batch windows to 60–80ms, add a cushion (e.g., 2–3s) for mobile flaky networks. Also enable the client-side reconnect logic that restarts where the session left off using continuation tokens.

[07:30] Derek S.: Continuation tokens — will those replay the same generation deterministically?

[07:36] Samira Ng: Not strictly deterministic unless you're using pinned RNG seeds; but continuation tokens include KV handles and last generated token so the runtime can resume without reprocessing the whole context — it's intended for UX resilience, not perfect deterministic replay.

[07:52] [Speaker 1: crosstalk, inaudible]

[08:00] Samira Ng: Next, timeout cascades — I'm simulating upstream service slowdown (embedding store takes 400ms occasionally) while high TPS is ongoing. Two things happen: one, per-request latency jumps and queuing grows; two, the routing policy activates a soft-fallback: requests start routing to standby model variants in other AZs and Redwood's circuit-breaker prevents overloading the embedding store by slowing down rate to that dependency.

[08:28] Maya R.: circuit-breaker to the embedding store — is that configable?

[08:32] Samira Ng: Yes, you can set dependency thresholds and policies: open after X consecutive failures, half-open probing, and so on. All visible in Console under Dependencies.

[08:44] Jordan Patel: Also important: our Optimize product will detect dependency-induced tail latencies and propose prefetching or caching strategies — e.g. precompute embeddings for heavy prefixes.

[08:58] Derek S.: For HelixEdge our peak is unpredictable; we'd like automatic scaling but also strong SLOs for the critical routes. How do you recommend we partition routes and SLAs?

[09:10] Samira Ng: Partition by business value: critical real-time agent sessions get pinned to dedicated pools with guaranteed CPU/GPU and lower batch windows. Less critical analytic jobs go to burstable shared capacity where batching windows widen. In Console you can map traffic by route to different deployment pools and set model fallbacks per route.

[09:30] [11m later: demo of routing UI omitted for brevity] Speaker 2: um — routing rules look straightforward.

[09:50] Samira Ng: Last section: the fallback playbook in ops. I'm going to walk through a three-step playbook we recommend when you see exponential tailback events:
1) Identify hot prefixes and enable targeted prefix eviction or compaction to increase effective KV hit rates.
2) If queuing latency exceeds soft SLOs, create a short-term route rule to route a percentage of traffic to a lower-cost model family for a canary (we use 5–10% initially).
3) If client timeouts rise, enable partial-output and engage aggressive keepalives and incrementally increase cache TTLs for frequently recomputed prefixes.

[10:30] Maya R.: Step 2 sounds risky for quality. How do we automate rollback?

[10:35] Samira Ng: Canary rollouts are automated with health checks: we monitor per-route quality metrics (similarity/regression), error rates, and user-facing metrics. If quality dips beyond a threshold (you define), the system re-routes traffic back and triggers an alert. You can also configure automatic fallback to the previous stable model.

[10:52] Derek S.: Can we do A/B where 5% goes to the fallback model but we also run similarity checks and only commit more traffic if similarity > 0.92?

[10:59] Samira Ng: Yep, that's a supported pattern — Optimize can run the similarity gating logic as part of the rollout.

[11:06] Jordan Patel: Quick note about billing: when you route to a quantized smaller model costs go down — Console shows token-level cost delta in the rollout UI so you can balance quality versus spend.

[11:20] Priya K.: Are there built-in dashboards for mobile client disconnect rate and partial-outputs?

[11:26] Samira Ng: Yes, under Observability -> Streaming you'll see per-route partial-output counts, slow-reader ratios, and session-level buffer events. We also emit structured audit logs for each fallback event.

[11:40] [Samira switches to an Optimize screen]

[11:45] Samira Ng: Optimize suggestions for your workload: increase prefix cache TTL for session groups with repetitive prompts; enable model family fallbacks for specific high-cost routes; and use dynamic batching limits that step up to wider windows only after a rate surge.

[12:02] Maya R.: Any gotchas around security and private deployment? We're considering VPC/private control plane for compliance.

[12:08] Jordan Patel: For private deployments we support the same runtime behaviors; the control plane runs either in a customer VPC or on-prem. Key differences: billing/export telemetry is optionally disabled, and audit logs can be streamed to your SIEM. There's an extra ops checklist for resource quotas and cross-AZ network tuning.

[12:26] Derek S.: Does fallback to cached responses risk returning PII?

[12:30] Samira Ng: Good callout — cached responses obey data-retention and redaction policies. You can configure caches to exclude PII-containing prefixes using a regex or NLP-based scrubber. We recommend enabling redaction at ingest if you're caching multi-tenant data.

[12:46] Priya K.: Something popped into my head — if we do partial output and then resume, is there a risk of duplicate tokens or hallucinated bridging?

[12:54] Samira Ng: Resume uses a continuation token with last emission index; the runtime avoids duplicating tokens but because generation is non-deterministic slight variations can appear. We provide heuristics to stitch outputs and a merge policy you can tune (aggressive de-dup vs permissive).

[13:12] [Short silence, then Derek asks about pricing]

[13:18] Derek S.: If we do a pilot and route 5% of traffic to a quantized family for 2 weeks, how is that billed?

[13:24] Jordan Patel: Usage-based billing as usual; for dedicated pools you can also do a short-term reserved commit. We'll send a pricing sketch in the follow-up.

[13:33] Samira Ng: Wrapping demo: I want to show a failed scenario where the fallback chain didn't help because the embedding store was overloaded and the cache miss rate spiked. Replay now — notice the two concurrent failures and then a manual override where we force-route to an archived responses store.

[13:50] [Simulated failure logs shown] Speaker 1: (inaudible) manual override triggered.

[14:00] Samira Ng: In that case we recommend an emergency route: fall back to a best-effort archived summary generator that has much lower cost and latency; it's better UX than 504s. We also record an incident in Console with all traces and a prepopulated Zoom log for post-mortem.

[14:20] Maya R.: This is useful. If we wanted Redwood to run that pilot for us, what would you need?

[14:26] Jordan Patel: We need a representative sample of your traffic (anonymized), peak TPS numbers, and a list of critical routes. We'll set up a dedicated pilot pool and run parallel benchmarking. I'll create a template for your traffic sample.

[14:38] Priya K.: And security docs?

[14:41] Jordan Patel: We'll share SOC2 + ISO artifacts, the VPC deployment checklist, and our KMS integration guide.

[14:48] Derek S.: timeline? We want results in ~2 weeks.

[14:52] Samira Ng: That's doable — for a lightweight pilot we can deliver an initial bench in 7 business days and a more comprehensive report in 10–14 days.

[15:03] [Short Q&A follows — partial quotes]

[15:05] Maya R.: what's the default buffer per session again?

[15:08] Samira Ng: default 8MB but you can tune per-route up to configured cluster limits.

[15:12] Derek S.: where do we set similarity threshold?

[15:15] Samira Ng: in Optimize -> Rollouts -> gating; default is 0.9 but we can set to 0.92 like you asked.

[15:23] Jordan Patel: I'll jot down the commitments: Jordan shares benchmarks, Samira runs mini benchmark, Derek shares TPS profile.

[15:30] Priya K.: Are there any logs or dashboards we can look at right away?

[15:34] Samira Ng: We'll share console screenshots and the live demo link plus a read-only Console access for the pilot.

[15:40] [Closing wrap] Jordan Patel: Great, next steps recap in chat. Anything else?

[15:45] Maya R.: No, looks good. Thanks everyone.

[15:48] Jordan Patel: Thanks all. We'll send the deck and the action item tracker.

[15:55] End of meeting notes.
